extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (general readers of Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: Passage from Plato's Republic (Book VI) describing the distinction between knowledge and opinion, the nature and virtues of the true philosopher, the parable of the ship, causes of corruption, and the proper education and role of philosopher-rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge vs. Opinion (being vs. not-being)
rubrics_metrics.description: The many ideas entertained by the multitude are 'in some region which is half-way between pure being and pure not-being' and are matters of opinion, not knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between knowledge (grasp of the absolute, eternal, immutable) and opinion (perception of the many and variable). Those who see absolutes may be said to know; those confined to particulars have opinion only. The passage repeatedly uses the contrast 'being' (the absolute) vs 'not-being' and locates ordinary beliefs in an intermediate flux.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical grasp of the eternal (qualification for guardianship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who can 'grasp the eternal and unchangeable' ought to be rulers because they can 'guard the laws and institutions' of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability to apprehend 'absolute beauty', 'absolute justice', and other Forms is presented as the central qualification for political guardianship; rulers should have the patterned vision of the other world to order laws about beauty, goodness, justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness (hatred of falsehood)
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher 'will never intentionally receive into their mind falsehood' and 'will love the truth'; the true lover of learning must 'desire all truth'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truthfulness is presented as integral and non-negotiable: the philosophical nature 'cannot help loving all that belongs or is akin to' its object (truth). A genuine philosopher must hate lies and intentionally seek truth in all things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of learning / intellectual appetite
rubrics_metrics.description: The true lover of learning from earliest youth 'must... desire all truth'; he should have 'a pleasure in learning' and be unwilling to persist in studies that cause pain with little progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophic vocation requires intrinsic pleasure in inquiry, endurance through dialectic difficulty, and study pursued as more than a pastime. Without this pleasure and persistence, one cannot be ranked among genuine philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and low bodily desire
rubrics_metrics.description: A true philosopher 'will hardly feel bodily pleasure' and is 'sure to be temperate and the reverse of covetous'; bodily appetites are subordinate to pleasures of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers prioritize soul-pleasures; temperance reduces distractions from philosophical pursuit and governance. The text links temperance with lack of covetousness and appropriate priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of meanness / magnificence of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be 'no secret corner of illiberality' in a philosopher; meanness is 'antagonistic' to a soul that longs for the whole of things — the philosopher has 'magnificence of mind'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnanimity and liberality (not petty or mean) are required traits; a philosophical soul cannot be petty if it truly apprehends the whole and divine aspects of reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage (not fearing death)
rubrics_metrics.description: One who contemplates 'all time and all existence' cannot 'account death fearful'; thus 'the cowardly and mean nature has no part in true philosophy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage is necessary for the philosopher: fear of death and cowardice are incompatible with true philosophic disposition and therefore with just rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice, gentleness, and social goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: A harmoniously constituted philosopher who is not covetous, mean, a boaster, or a coward 'can [not] ever be unjust or hard in his dealings'; signs like justice and gentleness distinguish the philosophical nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral virtues such as justice and gentleness follow from the harmonized soul; they are both signs and effects of true philosophical character and prerequisites for ruling well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good memory and quickness to learn
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher 'should have a good memory' and be 'quick to learn'; a soul which forgets 'cannot be ranked among genuine philosophic natures'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retention and capacity to learn are practical faculties required for the long intellectual training and public duties of rulers. 'Labouring in vain' due to forgetfulness undermines philosophical life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and graceful/harmonious mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher should be 'a naturally well-proportioned and gracious mind, which will move spontaneously towards the true being of everything.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic and psychic proportion (not merely physical) supports the correct orientation toward truth and virtue; disproportion is akin to falsehood, while truth is akin to proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of intellectual and moral excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers must unite the love of the eternal with other excellences (courage, temperance, magnificence, memory, apprehension) to be fit rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge alone is not enough: governance requires that epistemic virtues be combined with moral and practical virtues. The best place in the State belongs to those who unite knowledge and other excellences unless they fail in some other respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properly ordered, lifelong education (dialectic culminating in governance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should be pursued in a life-long, age-appropriate program: childhood study suited to youth, increasing 'gymnastics of the soul' as intellect matures, and study of dialectic in mature years; in old age they should range at will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes structured education: early cultivation of body for service of philosophy, then progressively rigorous intellectual training culminating in dialectic. Current practice (philosophy as spare-time hobby) is criticized; the State should order philosophical training so it does not ruin the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to corruption by popular opinion and sophists
rubrics_metrics.description: The public (the many) teach only 'the opinion of the many' and corrupt youth by praise/blame, applause, and by rewarding or punishing; 'Sophists' teach how to please the mob rather than truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers must be insulated or prepared against the 'overwhelming flood of popular opinion' and the corrupting influence of applause, wealth, rank, and sophistical education which teach conformity to tastes rather than knowledge of the good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of false imitators (philosophy's dishonourers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those unworthy of education enter philosophy for show (like 'bald little tinker' newly rich) and produce 'sophisms captivating to the ear' that dishonour true philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticate philosophical practice by substance not appearance: beware imitators who adopt philosophical trappings without the requisite nature or training; such impostors generate attractive but empty doctrines that degrade the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection from corrupting goods and social incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: External goods (beauty, wealth, strength, rank, great connections) and the philosopher's own virtues (courage, temperance, etc.) may, in alien conditions, 'destroy and distract from philosophy' and cause gifted minds to be ruined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excellent natures are especially vulnerable to corrupting environments; proper political structures and education must prevent distraction by honors and goods, since these can divert even the best natures into vice or vanity.
